lesson.title: Sterols and Cholesterol: Ring-Shaped Lipids That Fine-Tune the Membrane
lesson.summary: Sterols are lipids built around a distinctive four ring carbon skeleton rather than a long hydrocarbon chain, and cholesterol, the major animal sterol, wedges into cell membranes to buffer their fluidity while also serving as the raw material for steroid hormones and vitamin D.
lesson.body:
Not every lipid is built from long hydrocarbon chains attached to glycerol. Sterols form a structurally distinct branch of the lipid family, built instead around a rigid backbone of four fused carbon rings, three six membered rings and one five membered ring, known collectively as the steroid nucleus. Despite looking nothing like a fatty acid or a triglyceride, sterols are still classified as lipids because they share that defining lipid property discussed earlier: they are predominantly nonpolar and hydrophobic, made almost entirely of carbon and hydrogen arranged in a compact, water insoluble shape, with only small polar attachments here and there.

Cholesterol is the sterol you are most likely to have already heard of, and it is by far the most abundant sterol in animal cells. Its structure fits the general sterol pattern closely: the four ring steroid nucleus, a short branched hydrocarbon tail extending off one end, and a single hydroxyl group at the opposite end, on carbon three of the ring system. That one hydroxyl group is cholesterol's only meaningfully polar feature, small compared to the phosphate head of a phospholipid, but just present enough to give the molecule a mildly amphipathic character, a tiny polar head attached to an otherwise bulky, rigid, nonpolar body.

That mild amphipathic character is exactly what lets cholesterol embed itself within a phospholipid bilayer, oriented with its lone hydroxyl group facing outward near the polar phospholipid heads and its rigid ring system nestled among the fatty acid tails in the membrane's hydrophobic interior. Once inserted there, cholesterol acts as a kind of fluidity buffer for the membrane. At higher temperatures, cholesterol's rigid, flat ring system restricts how much the surrounding phospholipid tails can move around, preventing the membrane from becoming too fluid and leaky. At lower temperatures, cholesterol wedges between phospholipid tails and interrupts their ability to pack tightly against each other, preventing the membrane from becoming too stiff or from freezing into a solid gel. Few other molecules can push membrane fluidity in both directions depending on conditions, which makes cholesterol a genuinely distinctive regulatory lipid rather than just another structural filler.

Cholesterol also serves as the starting material from which the body synthesizes an entire family of other steroids, all sharing that same four ring nucleus with different attached groups. Steroid hormones such as estrogen, testosterone, and cortisol are all synthesized from cholesterol through successive enzymatic modifications, as are the bile acids the digestive system uses to emulsify dietary fat, and vitamin D, which the body can synthesize from a cholesterol derived precursor in the skin using ultraviolet light. Plants make their own related sterols, collectively called phytosterols, which resemble cholesterol structurally but are not identical to it and are not used by the human body in the same way.

Cholesterol is not soluble in blood plasma on its own, being far too hydrophobic, so it travels through the bloodstream packaged inside lipoprotein particles, commonly abbreviated LDL and HDL, which wrap cholesterol and other lipids in a shell of phospholipids and protein to make the whole package water compatible for transport between organs.
